paragraphs.source_en: Another example is In Itinen en haut (also known as Titerast n'Elias), a stone city on the Tassili Plateau, not far from Tin Aboteka. The site presents scattered paintings of the Pastoral and Camel periods but the Round Head paintings are concentrated only in a narrow wadi rather hidden by surrounding rocks. The morphology of this site is very different from the previous site of Tin Aboteka because In Itinen en haut is not visible from outside and only those who knew its exact position could have found the wadi containing the paintings. However, both sites present some fundamental similarities. As at Tin Aboteka, here we also find a shelter with a large composition presenting human figures with raised hands in a worshipping position, a large animal and a possible fantastic figure in the central part of the wall (Fig. 5-4).

units.source_en: However, both sites present some fundamental similarities.

As at Tin Aboteka, here we also find a shelter with a large composition presenting human figures with raised hands in a worshipping position, a large animal and a possible fantastic figure in the central part of the wall (Fig. 5-4).

paragraphs.source_en: Although the composition is very faded and some figures have almost completely disappeared, it is nevertheless clear that the unusual posture of the human figures, as well as two figures which are represented with elaborated body paintings, indicate a non everyday life scene. Furthermore, at least one of the large figures has two borders of different colours, red and brown; overlapping in some points but in other points they are slightly separated. As in the case of Tin Aboteka, this may be an ancient repainting of what was possibly considered an important figure. Significant for the relative chronology are the presence of cattle of the Pastoral style which were superimposed over these large Round Head figures.

paragraphs.source_en: In front of this composition, there is a large semicircle of stones, several metres wide (Fig. 5-5). As at Tin Aboteka, it is not a wall as it is very low; only one stone at a time has been positioned side by side. The age of the semicircle is prehistoric because all the stones present black patina, absent in the lower part covered by the soil. It could have been made by cattle herders but it does not seem to have been constructed for practical reasons such as a wind-break wall or an enclosure for animals, because it is not a real construction. The semicircle may have been made in a pre-Pastoral period. Since it is located right in front of the rock wall containing the enigmatic Round Head composition, the possibility of a direct connection to this image should be considered.
